title: Banks Near $15 Billion Loan for Anthropic Data Center Backed by Google Guarantees
excerpt: Morgan Stanley leads a bank consortium financing a massive Texas AI campus, with Google backstopping the deal in exchange for a 20% equity stake.
body:
• A Morgan Stanley-led bank consortium is in advanced talks to lend $15 billion to Nexus Data Centers for a massive AI campus in Hubbard, Texas, tied to Anthropic
  • Google will guarantee billions in lease and power-payment obligations if Anthropic defaults, receiving roughly 20% equity in the project in return
  • The campus will include a 1.6-gigawatt natural-gas power plant and be equipped with tensor processing units co-designed by Google and Broadcom
  • The deal represents one of the largest single AI infrastructure financings ever arranged, reflecting the scale of capital now flowing into the sector

The Deal Structure

A consortium of banks led by Morgan Stanley is in advanced talks to lend $15 billion to Nexus Data Centers for a new artificial intelligence campus in Hubbard, Texas, according to the Wall Street Journal and Reuters, citing people familiar with the matter.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=rQwmzxpMOpc

The financing package consists of a $14 billion bridge loan and a revolving credit facility. Evercore arranged the transaction and serves as Nexus's sole financial adviser. The deal represents one of the largest single-project AI infrastructure financings ever assembled.

Nexus Data Centers, a relatively new developer, would build the campus roughly 80 miles south of Dallas-Fort Worth. Public permit filings describe a 491,380-square-foot data center building with an estimated construction cost of $400 million, along with 600 megawatts of on-site natural gas generation on a roughly 2,900-acre site.

Google's Backstop

The financing hinges on Google's willingness to put its investment-grade balance sheet behind the project. Alphabet's Google unit has agreed to guarantee billions of dollars of Anthropic's lease and power-payment commitments in the event the AI startup defaults, according to the reports.

"Google's support was limited and covered the minimum amount the banks required to get the financing done."

— Wall Street Journal, citing people familiar with the matter

The guarantees cover four data-center leases Anthropic has signed, along with corresponding power-purchase agreements tied to a behind-the-meter power plant. In exchange, Google is expected to receive an equity stake of roughly 20% in the data-center and power project.

The structure effectively allows lenders to underwrite Google's credit profile rather than Anthropic's, making the debt far cheaper to issue than it would be based on the AI startup's balance sheet alone.

Hardware and Power

Anthropic plans to fill the facility with tensor processing units — chips co-designed by Google and Broadcom. The TPUs will be financed through a separate vendor-financing deal Anthropic has struck with Broadcom, keeping the chip procurement off the main project's balance sheet.

The campus will have its own natural-gas-fired power plant capable of generating 1.6 gigawatts of electricity, enough to power roughly 1.2 million homes. The scale reflects the enormous energy demands of training and running large AI models.

AI's Infrastructure Arms Race

The Anthropic financing is part of a broader wave of AI infrastructure deals reshaping corporate finance. Meta recently raised more than $27 billion for its Hyperion data-center campus in Louisiana through a joint venture with Blue Owl Capital. Microsoft, Amazon, and Oracle have each announced multi-billion-dollar data center buildouts across the United States and internationally.

Morgan Stanley has emerged as a lead arranger for several of these deals, using project finance techniques traditionally applied to power plants and toll roads to fund data center campuses backed by Big Tech credit guarantees.

Anthropic, the maker of the Claude AI assistant, has raised more than $20 billion in venture capital and was recently valued at $175 billion. The company declined to comment on the financing. Google and Morgan Stanley did not respond to requests for comment.
